questions.question: Q: What determines whether a rock deforms in a brittle or ductile manner?

points.text: Temperature, pressure (depth), strain rate and rock type. High temperature and pressure (great depth) favour ductile deformation (folding). Low temperature and pressure (shallow depth) and rapid stress favour brittle deformation (faulting).

questions.question: Q: How does a normal fault differ from a reverse fault?

points.text: A normal fault forms under tension, the hanging wall moves down relative to the footwall. A reverse fault forms under compression, the hanging wall moves up relative to the footwall.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between a joint and a fault?

points.text: A joint is a fracture with no movement along it. A fault is a fracture where the rock blocks have moved relative to each other.

questions.question: Q: What type of stress produces a strike-slip fault?

points.text: Shear stress, forces acting parallel to the fault plane cause the blocks to slide horizontally past each other (e.g. San Andreas Fault).

questions.question: Q: Why do rocks fold rather than fracture deep in the crust?

points.text: At great depth, high temperatures and pressures make rocks more ductile (plastic). They can bend and flow slowly under stress rather than breaking, producing folds instead of faults.
